facts.fact: Using the page's illustrative coffee shop example, a customer spending $5 per visit who visits four times a week for three years generates $3,120 in total revenue.

facts.fact: The page's simple CLV formula is Average Purchase Value x Purchase Frequency x Average Customer Lifespan.
facts.quote: CLV = Average Purchase Value x Purchase Frequency x Average Customer Lifespan

facts.fact: In the page's illustrative hair salon example, a $75 average ticket, 6 visits per year, and 4 years of retention yield a CLV of $1,800.
In the page's illustrative HVAC example, a $350 average service call, 1.5 calls per year, and an 8-year lifespan yield a CLV of $4,200.
In the page's illustrative restaurant example, a $35 average check, 18 visits per year, and a 3-year lifespan yield a CLV of $1,890.
Applying a 60% profit margin to the page's salon example reduces its CLV from $1,800 to $1,080.
The page's industry benchmark table estimates HVAC/plumbing CLV at $1,500-10,000, based on average transaction of $250-500, 1-2 calls per year, and 6-10 years of lifespan.

facts.fact: In the article's illustrative example, Sarah's five customers, acquired with a $400 Instagram spend, are projected to generate over $5,700 in profit over four years.

facts.fact: The article says a business will have enough data to calculate a preliminary CLV after three to six months of tracking.
facts.quote: After three to six months, you'll have enough data to calculate a preliminary CLV.

facts.fact: The article recommends recalculating CLV at minimum once a year, and every quarter if the business is growing quickly or has made significant changes to pricing, services, or retention strategies.
facts.quote: At minimum, once a year. If your business is growing quickly or you've made significant changes to pricing, services, or retention strategies, recalculate every quarter.

facts.fact: The article states that a CLV:CAC ratio above 5:1 can signal that a business is underinvesting in growth.
facts.quote: a CLV:CAC ratio above 5:1 can signal that you're underinvesting in growth.

facts.fact: In the article's illustrative example, a CLV of $5,000 with a CAC of $100 gives room to spend more aggressively on marketing.
facts.quote: If your CLV is $5,000 and your CAC is only $100, you have room to spend more aggressively on marketing.

facts.fact: The article's illustrative example says a 20% first-purchase discount is easy to justify when a customer will spend $2,000 over three years.
facts.quote: A 20% discount that brings someone in the door is easy to justify when you know that customer will spend $2,000 over three years.

facts.fact: The article states that CLV and LTV are used interchangeably and refer to the same concept, the total value a customer generates over their relationship with a business.
facts.quote: They're the same thing. CLV (customer lifetime value) and LTV (lifetime value) are used interchangeably across marketing and business literature.
